nature-res-248.title: Natural resources: where every product begins
nature-res-248.text: Trace any man-made product back far enough and it ends in nature. A natural resource is something drawn from nature and used with few changes: sunlight, air, water, land, minerals, plants and wildlife. Economists count these among the basic inputs to production, the {{ref:nature-econ-086}}. Some resources are restored by natural processes. Many extractive industries, though, rely on materials that can be dug or pumped out only once. That difference shapes much of what follows. Who gets these resources sits at the center of many economic and political confrontations, and the fights sharpen as scarcity increases. Extraction is also a major source of human rights violations and environmental damage. In 1982 the United Nations' {{ref:nature-gov-056}} recognized the need to protect nature from further depletion by human activity. A whole field now asks how managing land, water, soil, plants and animals affects quality of life, for people alive today and for generations to come.

nature-res-204.title: Resource depletion: using nature faster than it returns
nature-res-204.text: The problem is centuries old, but it became a major concern only in the 1970s. Resource depletion is the using up of a natural resource faster than it can be replaced. It takes many shapes: degraded wetlands and other ecosystems, eroded soil, drained underground water stores, and fish caught faster than they can breed. Its roots lie in colonialism and industrialization. With the Industrial Revolution, new technology and economic growth raised demand, and extraction of every kind of resource rose sharply. Markets register some of this. A resource's value depends on how much of it exists in nature and how costly it is to extract, and under {{ref:nature-econ-360}} scarcer resources become more valuable. The burden is unevenly shared. Wealthy nations have been described as outsourcing depletion to poorer nations, which suffer the greatest ecosystem losses. Economists often explain why depletion happens with the {{ref:nature-econ-606}}, where users of a shared resource each have reason to take more before others do.

nature-res-209.title: Non-renewable resources: the stock that does not come back
nature-res-209.text: Coal, oil and gas took thousands of years to form, and people use them far faster than that. A non-renewable resource, also called a finite resource, is a natural resource that nature cannot replace quickly enough to keep up with use. Minerals and metal ores, fossil fuels, and the water in some underground stores all qualify. Ore deposits form only where geological processes concentrate metals, which takes tens of thousands to millions of years. On human time-frames, deposits near the surface will not come back. Fossil fuels remain the main energy source humans use today. Some argue carbon fuel is practically inexhaustible if methane hydrates on the sea floor are counted. No one knows whether they can be extracted at a viable cost. Economists put the idea simply: using more today means less is available tomorrow. David Ricardo argued that a mineral's price should rise over time. In his view the costliest mine in use sets the price, and cheaper mines earn a differential rent. Without regulation, people and firms tend to keep using these resources, because the easier, cheaper option is often not the environmentally friendly one.

nature-res-212.title: Renewable resources: the stock that regrows, if allowed
nature-res-212.text: A forest can regrow and a fish population can breed back, but only if people let them. A renewable resource, also called a flow resource, replaces what is used through natural reproduction or other recurring processes within a human time scale. Some sources, such as sun, wind, moving water and geothermal heat, are practically infinite and cannot be depleted. Resources whose recovery will probably never outlast a human time scale get a name of their own, {{ref:nature-res-215}}. Water, forests, plants and animals stay renewable only as long as they are monitored, protected and conserved. Water shows the catch. It is renewable only when its use is carefully controlled, and underground water pumped far faster than it recharges counts as non-renewable. Overuse is not new: deforestation, overgrazing and fishing too hard were already large problems in early modern times. Unregulated industrial growth endangers these resources, which must be managed so use does not exceed nature's capacity to replenish them. Fisheries show how far it can go, since an unregulated industry can wipe a renewable resource out completely. Even clean energy has a hidden draw: building renewable energy devices uses mined metals and land.

nature-res-213.title: Natural resource economics: running an economy within nature's limits
nature-res-213.text: Fish, trees and ore: for decades, those three made up the core of the subject. Natural resource economics is the branch of economics that studies the supply, demand and sharing out of the Earth's natural resources. It began when researchers mainly wanted to know how to exploit stocks of resources commercially in the best way. Its traditional curriculum centered on models of fisheries, forests and mineral extraction. Its classic topics include welfare theory, how land is used, pollution control, resource extraction, valuing what markets do not price, exhaustibility and sustainability. Environmental economics was once a separate subject. More recently air, water, the global climate and environmental resources in general have become important to policy, and interest has moved beyond commercial exploitation alone. The field's main aim now is to understand nature's role in the economy, so resources can be managed sustainably and stay available to future generations. Put simply, it asks how to run an economy within the ecological limits of the Earth's resources. Not everyone is satisfied. {{ref:nature-eecon-059}} criticizes the field for focusing mainly on efficient allocation, and less on fair distribution and on the scale of the economy.

nature-res-220.title: Exploiting natural resources to fuel growth
nature-res-220.text: In the 19th century, mining, steam power and machinery pushed extraction far beyond pre-industrial levels. The exploitation of natural resources means using them, often non-renewable or limited ones, to drive economic growth or development. Two forces speed it up: better technology, which makes extraction faster, and rising consumption and consumerism, which raise demand. The costs often land on others. Exploitation tends to bring environmental damage, human insecurity and social conflict. Foreign industries often take raw materials from developing countries, and local communities see little of the profit. Soil shows the scale. The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) finds that about 33% of the Earth's soils are moderately to highly degraded, and that more than 90% could be by 2050. The rule for sustainable use is simple to state: consume a resource no faster than it is supplied. Not everyone accepts that resources are finite at all. The economist Julian Simon argued that substitution, {{ref:nature-eecon-038}} and new technology make scarcity ever more doubtful, a view others strongly dispute.

nature-res-234.title: Malthusianism: when population outruns food
nature-res-234.text: In 1798 Thomas Robert Malthus published {{ref:nature-hist-011}}, and its gloomy logic still carries his name. Malthusianism holds that population can grow exponentially while food and other resources grow only steadily. Living standards therefore fall until population declines. Better technology could raise resources, he argued, but the extra abundance would fuel more births until each person's share fell back. The predicted end is a Malthusian catastrophe, or trap: famine or war once population outpaces farm output. The pre-industrial record fits. From 1 to 1500 AD better technology raised population density but not living standards. A laborer's daily wage bought about 15 pounds of wheat in ancient Babylonia and 13 in England in 1800. After World War II, mechanized farming and the Green Revolution greatly raised crop yields, and most developed countries' populations grew more slowly than productivity. Critics from Ricardo onward disputed the theory, and the 20th century's growth did not bring the predicted catastrophe. Still, many models of resource depletion are Malthusian in shape, predicting that consumption will outrun new supply.

nature-res-218.title: Economic rent: income that rewards no effort
nature-res-218.text: Some income rewards no effort at all. Economic rent is any payment to the owner of a factor of production, such as land, beyond what is needed to bring that factor into use. Unlike economic profit, rent counts as unearned income, and competition cannot wipe it out. In farming and extraction, rent arises because land, oil and minerals are scarce and unevenly spread. Scarcity rent is paid for identical land when supply falls short of demand. Differential rent is the surplus that better land earns over the poorest land in use. Governments can collect part of it as royalties on minerals, oil and gas. Henry George argued that taxing unearned land rent would not distort economic activity, and proposed it as the main source of public revenue. Later, public choice theorists used the word for wealth transferred through rights the state grants, the origin of the term rent seeking.

nature-res-200.title: The resource curse: riches that hold countries back
nature-res-200.text: In 1711 The Spectator observed that the most plentiful countries often had the poorest living. Much later, Richard Auty gave the pattern a name. In 1993 he used the term resource curse for mineral-rich countries that grew more slowly than countries without plentiful resources. The idea is that countries rich in oil and minerals often see slower economic growth, weaker democracy or worse development than countries with fewer resources. A 1995 study by Jeffrey Sachs and Andrew Warner found a strong link between resource abundance and poor growth. The stakes are wide. The International Monetary Fund (IMF) counts 51 countries as resource-rich, meaning nonrenewable resources supply at least 20% of exports or 20% of government revenue. Of these, 29 are low or lower-middle income. Several mechanisms are proposed. Oil and mineral prices swing widely, so revenues jump and crash, disrupting planning and debt payments. Extraction tends to form an enclave with few links to the rest of the economy. Its high profits draw the best workers and investment away from other industries. Economies dominated by extraction also tend to be less democratic and more corrupt, and petroleum is the resource most consistently tied to weaker institutions. Yet there is no academic consensus. Studies with empirical support reach contradictory findings, and most experts think the curse is not universal, striking certain kinds of countries under certain conditions.

nature-res-231.title: Ecological yield: the harvest an ecosystem can spare
nature-res-231.text: A forest can give up some wood each year and still stand. Ecological yield is the amount of an ecosystem's growth that can be harvested while still letting it recover. It is most often measured in forests, where sustainable harvesting takes no more wood in a year than grew that year in a given patch. Take more than is renewed and the ecosystem's carrying capacity shrinks over time. The figure can only be estimated, and it depends on the recovery period chosen: three years' sustainable harvest is not necessarily three times one year's. Firms that borrow to buy rights to land may owe debts that demand more yield than the land can renew. Food chains shrink yield fast. Only about 10% of biomass passes from prey to predator, so 100 kg of plants may yield 10 kg of plant-eaters and 1 kg of meat-eaters. In 1986 Vitousek and colleagues estimated that humans use 50 billion tons of photosynthetic biomass a year, 20% to 40% of the Earth's photosynthesis. Measuring ecological footprints accurately requires estimating this yield.

nature-res-244.title: Sustainable yield: harvesting without shrinking the stock
nature-res-244.text: A stock of fish or trees can be harvested forever, as long as the harvest stays within one limit. Sustainable yield is the amount of a renewable resource people can harvest without over-harvesting or damaging it. Formally, it is the ecological yield that can be taken without shrinking the natural capital itself. It applies only to renewable resources, because extracting non-renewable ones always reduces natural capital. It is often calculated at half the carrying capacity, a level at which a stock can be harvested and still regrow. A forest hit by a natural disaster needs more of its own growth to recover, so its sustainable yield falls. The idea is used mostly for forests, fisheries and underground water, where a 'safe yield' marks the pumping rate beyond which the store is overdrawn. After fish were overharvested in the mid-1850s, {{ref:nature-res-013}} became a reference point for managing fisheries. Critics say forest harvesting planned this way values only wood, changes landscapes and reduces biodiversity, and some call the whole idea anthropocentric, centered on human needs.

nature-res-232.title: The Hubbert curve: how a resource rises, peaks and falls
nature-res-232.text: In 1956 the geologist M. King Hubbert presented the American Petroleum Institute with a curve and a forecast. The Hubbert curve is a bell-shaped curve approximating how a resource's production rate rises, peaks and falls over time. Using the 1948 peak in oil well discoveries, Hubbert predicted that oil production in the contiguous United States would peak around 1970. After an early-1970s peak, US output followed his curve for 35 years. Then new extraction methods pushed it to a record 10.07 million barrels a day in November 2017. Real production curves are often lopsided like this, bent by new techniques, competing resources and government rules. Strictly, the curve is a symmetric logistic distribution, often confused with the normal, or Gaussian, curve it resembles. It has been applied to natural gas, coal, uranium, copper, helium and water. A modified version fits any resource harvested faster than it is replaced.

nature-res-222.title: Peak oil: the top of the world's production curve
nature-res-222.text: Every oilfield eventually runs down: output rises, levels off, then falls. Peak oil is the point when world petroleum production reaches its highest rate, after which it declines for good. The same rise-and-fall assumption underlies Hubbert's peak theory. Predictions of the peak range from 2025 to after 2050. Forecasting it has proved humbling. Predictions in 2007 and 2009 of an imminent peak were followed by record production in 2018 and 101.73 million barrels per day in 2023. Conventional oil is recognized to have peaked around 2005–2006, but rapid growth in US tight oil since 2008 has kept total output rising. Reserves are finite; the key question is whether extraction pays at current prices. Critics argue that as prices rise, harder sources become worth tapping, so the world is running out only of cheap oil. The theory remains controversial. Still, a sharp fall in supply could raise the cost of transport, food, heating and electricity everywhere, because modern farming depends on fuel and chemicals made from oil.

nature-res-239.title: Resource rent: what nature pays after the bills
nature-res-239.text: Sell a resource's output, pay every cost of getting it out, including a normal return, and what is left is resource rent. It is the economic rent earned from natural resources such as minerals, oil reserves, rivers, waterfalls, coastal space and wind. It comes in several kinds. Differential, or Ricardian, rent comes from better sites: at the same price, a coal firm with costs of $20/t earns more rent than one with $30/t. Scarcity rent arises because extracting a finite resource today leaves less for later. If oil's price rises from $50 to $70 while costs stay at $30, rent per barrel rises from $20 to $40. Entrepreneurial rent, a form of {{ref:nature-res-219}}, comes from skill or investment that cuts costs or raises the price. Some call resource rents a 'natural dividend' that should belong to the people who own the resources. In fisheries, the catch that makes this rent largest is {{ref:nature-res-084}}, and catching more only shrinks the rent.

nature-res-221.title: Hotelling's rule: why oil in the ground should gain value
nature-res-221.text: An owner of oil faces a choice each year: extract now, or leave it in the ground and sell later. In 1931 {{ref:nature-hist-062}} published the classic answer in the Journal of Political Economy. Hotelling's rule describes how the net price of a non-renewable resource should change over time when its owner extracts it to earn the most rent. The net price is the selling price minus costs. With efficient extraction it rises each period by a percentage equal to the discount rate, which maximizes the present value of the resource. The rule also implies that efficient use of a resource that cannot be added to, under stable conditions, ends in its depletion. The largest rent obtainable while emptying the stock is the subject of {{ref:nature-res-252}}. That rent equals the net price, and equals the shadow value of the natural capital still in the ground. L. C. Gray had published a similar result for a single mine owner in 1914.

nature-res-249.title: Sorting natural resources four ways
nature-res-249.text: Coal and oil count as living resources, at least by origin. Natural resources can be sorted by origin, stage of development, renewability and ownership. By origin, biotic resources come from living things, including fossil fuels formed from decayed organic matter. Abiotic ones come from non-living material such as land, water and ores. By stage, potential resources are known but unused, like unextracted petroleum, while actual resources are surveyed and in use. By ownership, they can be individual, community, national or international, as with international waters.

nature-res-229.title: Dutch disease: when a boom hollows out the rest
nature-res-229.text: In 1959 the Netherlands discovered the Groningen gas field, and Dutch manufacturing then declined. In 1977 The Economist coined a name for the pattern: Dutch disease. It describes the apparent link between a boom in one sector, such as natural resources, and a decline in others such as manufacturing or agriculture. The mechanism runs through the currency. Boom revenues strengthen it, making the country's other exports dearer abroad and imports cheaper, so those sectors lose ground. Any large inflow of foreign currency can do this, including foreign aid and foreign direct investment. Trade theory says resource-rich countries should specialize in extraction, but this backfires when the resource runs down, because manufacturing cannot return as fast as it left. Diagnosis is hard. Still, very large, unexpected oil and gas discoveries do on average seem to raise the real exchange rate and shrink lagging sectors. Remedies include saving boom revenue abroad in a {{ref:nature-res-243}}, running budget surpluses, and investing in education and infrastructure for the lagging sectors.

nature-res-233.title: Ricardo's law of rent
nature-res-233.text: 'Corn is not high because a rent is paid, but rent is paid because corn is high.' With that line David Ricardo turned an everyday assumption upside down. Around 1809 he formulated the law of rent, set out fully in On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation. It says the rent of a piece of land equals the extra output it produces compared with the best land available rent-free, using the same labor and capital. Ricardo's example used plots yielding 100, 90 and 80 units of corn. Once the 90-unit plot must be farmed too, the best plot earns a rent of 10 units. The output of the best rent-free land is called the margin of production. The law is the origin of the term Ricardian rent. It applies to urban and rural land alike, and to any natural factor of production that is privately owned. Ricardian rent differs from contract rent, the payments tenants actually make for using others' property.

nature-res-237.title: Marine resources: what the oceans offer
nature-res-237.text: The oceans hold far more than fish. Marine resources are the physical and biological things in the oceans that are useful to people. They include marine biodiversity, ecosystem services from coasts and coral reefs, minerals from deep sea mining, and marine renewable energy. The term spread through the UN goal set in 2015 to conserve and sustainably use the oceans, seas and marine resources, {{ref:nature-gov-027}}. Sustainable fisheries contributed around 0.1% of global GDP per year.

nature-res-245.title: The blue economy: making a living from water
nature-res-245.text: In 2023 the European Union's blue economy employed nearly 4.9 million people and added €263 billion in gross value added. The blue economy is the economic use of oceans, lakes, rivers and coasts, generally with an emphasis on using their resources sustainably. There is no agreed definition. The World Bank calls it sustainable use of ocean resources for growth, livelihoods and jobs while preserving the health of ocean ecosystems. It spans fisheries, fish farming, shipping and tourism, plus newer activities such as offshore renewable energy, {{ref:nature-nbs-034}} and seabed mining. It also covers unpriced ocean services such as storing carbon, coastal protection and biodiversity. Mangrove forests show what is at stake. They support more than 4 million fishers and protect coasts, yet 0.5% have been lost each year on average since the 2000s. The term spread after a UN conference on sustainable growth in 2012, {{ref:nature-hist-008}}. Misleading claims about effects on waters have their own label, {{ref:nature-nbs-080}}.

nature-res-207.title: Fixed stock or opportunity cost: two ways to count what is left
nature-res-207.text: How much of a mineral is left? The answer depends on what is counted. One view treats a mineral resource as a fixed physical stock that use steadily draws down. The other measures its usable amount through its price and opportunity cost. Tilton and Lagos (2007) argued the second view is better, because price and opportunity cost represent the quantity people can actually use. Since total stocks and future markets are unknown, most economists doubt that physical scarcity is a good guide to availability. How best to model depletion remains an open debate.

nature-res-208.title: Underground water that will not refill in time
nature-res-208.text: Less than six percent of the world's water is replenished on a human timescale of 50 years. Much underground water refills far too slowly to be replaced within human lifetimes, so it is effectively non-renewable. Farming leans on it heavily: 16–33% of the underground water used for agriculture is non-renewable. Pumping too much lowers water levels and can dry up streams, harming the ecosystems on the surface. {{ref:nature-res-133}} looks at this hidden store in more depth.

nature-res-227.title: Cornucopianism: the case for endless plenty
nature-res-227.text: In Greek mythology the cornucopia, the horn of plenty, never runs dry. Cornucopianism borrows the name for the view that advancing technology can keep meeting humanity's material needs, so growth is practically unlimited. Its believers, the 'boomsters', are set against Malthusian 'doomsters'. The economist Julian Simon made the classic case in his 1981 book The Ultimate Resource. Humans, he argued, have always found ways to develop resources past nearly any roadblock. Free markets were essential to his story: when shortage raises a resource's price, research into cheaper alternatives follows. Few people call themselves cornucopians. The label is mostly used by critics who find the view over-optimistic. Lindsey Grant and Naomi Oreskes reject its arguments as flawed. Oreskes points out that many key innovations came from government action, and that technological progress has not stopped the climate crisis.

nature-res-242.title: The Simon–Ehrlich wager: betting on scarcity
nature-res-242.text: On 29 September 1980 a biologist and an economist bet on the future of the planet. Paul Ehrlich, author of {{ref:nature-hist-020}} (1968), expected a growing population to outstrip resources. Julian Simon bet that raw material prices would not rise in the long run. Ehrlich chose five metals, copper, chromium, nickel, tin and tungsten, buying $200 of each on paper. By 29 September 1990 all five had fallen in inflation-adjusted price, even though world population grew by more than 800 million. Ehrlich paid Simon $576.07. The verdict is less tidy than the payout. Over 1980–2011 Simon would have lost on four of the five metals. One study found he would have won in only 38.4% of periods from 1900 to 2008. Some analysts conclude that luck mattered more than expertise, and that the bet does not prove there are no environmental limits to growth. Observers still disagree on what it shows, since the result depends heavily on the period chosen. Simon later declined Ehrlich and Schneider's offer to bet on 15 environmental trends; he would have lost on 11.

nature-res-210.title: Land: the resource no one can make more of
nature-res-210.text: Land can be reused endlessly, but no one can create more of it on demand. Economists therefore treat it as a fixed resource whose supply cannot respond to price: in their terms, its supply is perfectly inelastic. Unlike machines and other capital goods, land and non-renewable resources cannot be produced or increased. Whether land surface counts as renewable or non-renewable depends on what it is compared with.

openers.res: Every economy runs on things taken from nature, from sunlight and water to minerals, plants and wildlife. Some of these renew themselves within a human lifetime; others, once used, are gone for good. Natural resource economics studies how such resources are supplied, demanded and shared out, and why owning them can enrich a country or, surprisingly often, hold it back. This part follows that thread from minerals and fish to the payments that flow to whoever owns scarce land and ore.
openers.renewable-and-non-renewable-resources: Some resources come back and some do not. Forests, fish and other living things can replace what is taken within a human lifetime, while minerals, once used, are gone. This chapter follows that dividing line and what happens when people draw down a resource faster than it can recover. Along the way it meets the old fear that population will outrun food, the bell-shaped curve that tracks a resource's rise and fall, and the puzzle of why mineral wealth so often fails the countries that hold it.
